summary: Describes private SIP extensions that let a network of trusted servers assert the identity of authenticated users, including the P-Asserted-Identity header, and applies existing privacy mechanisms. It works only inside a domain with agreed policies and is not a general identity solution. It was later updated by RFCs 5876 and 8217.

eli5.summary: Inside a trusted club, the doorman can write your verified name on a badge. This lets phone servers in a trusted network mark calls with who made them, without announcing it everywhere.

questions: how do trusted sip networks assert identity
what is the sip privacy id token
what is a sip trust domain
subtitle: How servers inside a trusted SIP network can vouch for who a caller is, and hide that from outsiders when the caller asks.

tldr.problem: Telephony services over SIP need trusted network elements to pass on the identity of subscribers, yet withhold it from untrusted parties when the user wants privacy.
tldr.mechanism: A proxy that has authenticated the user inserts a P-Asserted-Identity header and forwards it to trusted nodes. A new id token in the Privacy header tells it to strip that header before the message leaves the Trust Domain.
tldr.outcome: It works only inside an administrative domain with agreed policies, and the asserted identities are not cryptographically certified. It is not a general identity or privacy model for the Internet.

facts.label: Values per header
facts.value: one or two (a sip/sips URI and/or a tel URI)

today: RFC 3325 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 5876 and RFC 8217. Its own text says it is meant only for closed, trusted deployments.

sections.title: Applicability and the Trust Domain
sections.content:
These are private extensions to SIP that let a network of trusted servers assert the identity of end users or end systems, and convey a user's privacy request. They apply only inside a Trust Domain as defined in RFC 3324: nodes that users and end systems explicitly trust to assert each party's identity publicly and to withhold it outside the domain when privacy is requested.

All nodes in a Trust Domain T must be known to comply with a set of specifications called Spec(T). It must cover how users are authenticated, how communication is secured between nodes and between user agents and nodes, how hosts are determined to be in the domain, the default privacy handling when no Privacy header is present, compliance with SIP and with this document, and privacy handling for identity.

The RFC states it does NOT offer a general privacy or identity model for inter-domain use or the Internet at large. The asserted identities are not cryptographically certified, so they are subject to forgery, replay and falsification in any architecture that does not meet the Trust Domain requirements. An example deployment would be a closed network that emulates a traditional circuit switched telephone network.
sections.eli5: This only works inside a club where everyone has agreed to the same rules. Outside the club, the badge means nothing.

sections.title: The Idea in Brief
sections.content:
Providers offering telephony over IP need services such as Calling Identity Delivery, Calling Identity Delivery Blocking and the ability to trace the originator of a call. Baseline SIP supports each alone, but not certain combinations. A caller who hides behind limited information in the From header will not be identifiable by recipients, and masking identity at the originating user agent breaks services like call trace.

The fix is a new header field, P-Asserted-Identity, holding a URI (commonly a SIP URI) and an optional display name. A proxy that has authenticated the originating user, for example with Digest authentication, can insert it and forward it to other trusted proxies. The RFC applies the general SIP privacy mechanism of RFC 3323 to this problem.
sections.eli5: If a caller hides their name on purpose, the phone company still needs to know who it is. So the company adds its own verified note that only trusted friends can read.

sections.title: Proxy and User Agent Behavior
sections.content:
When a proxy gets a message from a node it does not trust and wants to add a P-Asserted-Identity header, it MUST authenticate the originator first. If the message comes from a trusted node, the proxy can use any existing asserted identity as if it had authenticated the user itself. A proxy MAY add a header containing at most one SIP or SIPS URI and at most one tel URL. From an untrusted source, an existing SIP or SIPS URI MUST be replaced by a single one or removed, and likewise for a tel URI.

A user can also send a P-Preferred-Identity header to a proxy as a hint for which of several valid identities to assert. The proxy MAY use it, or build its own header, or reject the request, for example with 403 Forbidden. The proxy MUST remove the user-provided header before forwarding. User agents MUST NOT send it unless the message goes directly to a proxy they trust.

On the receiving side, a user agent server typically shows the asserted identity to its user, but if the previous element is not trusted it MUST NOT use the header in any way. A UA inside the Trust Domain can use the value freely but must not forward it outside the domain if the user asked for privacy.
sections.eli5: The doorman must check your ID before writing a badge. You may suggest which name to put on it, but the doorman decides, and takes your suggestion note away afterwards.

sections.title: Requesting Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC adds a new privacy type, id, to the Privacy header defined by RFC 3323. If Privacy: id is present, proxies MUST remove all P-Asserted-Identity header values before forwarding to elements that are not trusted. If the Privacy value is none, the proxy MUST NOT remove them. A user who wants several kinds of privacy MUST list all of them in the one Privacy header.

When there is no Privacy header, a proxy forwarding to an untrusted element MAY keep or remove the header; that is a policy of the Trust Domain and MUST be specified in Spec(T). The RFC recommends not removing it unless local privacy policy prevents it, because removal may break services that rely on asserted identity. It also STRONGLY RECOMMENDS that all users have access to privacy services, since otherwise the identity may be disclosed without the user's wishing it.
sections.eli5: If you say 'keep my name private', the doorman peels the badge off before you leave the club. If you say nothing, the club rules decide.

sections.title: Header Syntax
sections.content:
P-Asserted-Identity carries the user's identity as verified by authentication, among trusted SIP entities (typically intermediaries). Each value is exactly one name-addr or addr-spec. There may be one or two values: a single value MUST be a sip, sips or tel URI, and two values MUST be one sip or sips URI plus one tel URI.

P-Preferred-Identity has the same value rules, but travels from a user agent to a trusted proxy to say which identity the user would like asserted. The privacy value is written priv-value = "id". The syntax uses the ABNF of RFC 2234, and the document adds entries for both headers to Table 2 of RFC 3261.

An example from the RFC:

P-Asserted-Identity: "Cullen Jennings" <sip:fluffy@cisco.com>
sections.eli5: The badge can show one or two names, such as an internet address and a phone number, and nothing else. The privacy request is just the short word id.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls this a partial treatment of identity and privacy in SIP. It gives users no way to share identity information end to end without a trusted service provider. Information marked private can be inspected by any intermediary in the Trust Domain, and it is secured by transitive trust, which is only as reliable as the weakest link in the chain of trust.

A trusted entity that sends a message carrying someone's identity in P-Asserted-Identity MUST protect it against eavesdropping and interception. Hop-by-hop transport or network layer security such as TLS or IPSec with appropriate cipher suites can satisfy this. The RFC also gives a non-normative example Spec(T) that requires Digest authentication and mutually authenticated TLS between nodes.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the club can see the badges, so the club is only as safe as its least careful member. Messages between members should travel in sealed envelopes.

messages.label: INVITE
messages.note: Privacy: id and a P-Preferred-Identity hint.

messages.label: INVITE + P-Asserted-Identity
messages.note: Trusted node, so the asserted identity stays.

messages.label: INVITE, identity removed
messages.note: Untrusted node: the asserted identity is stripped; Privacy: id remains.
